:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ given that $f(x,y) = 3x\ln y + 2ye^x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+2{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3x}{y}+2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding Partial Derivatives of Two-Variable Functions

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y) = y^2\ln{x},$ express $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ as the limit of a difference quotient.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}\right).
$$

Since $f(x) = y^2 \ln{x},$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y) = y^2\ln(x+h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left( \dfrac{y^2\ln(x+h) -y^2\ln{x} }{h}\right).
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Partial Derivatives as Limits of Difference Quotients

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y) = x^2y^2+\sin{x}\cos{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(\pi,2\pi).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,2\pi )} & =2\cdot \pi \cdot (2\pi )^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4{\pi }^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =8{\pi }^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$
